name: Lottery
seoDesc: Lottery: work out your result from number of matches and the matches with bonus pool. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary:
Supply number of matches, the matches with bonus pool, the pool drawn and the drawn match and the Lottery calculator solves for the answer. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number.

Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Lottery calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lottery calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in number of matches, the matches with bonus pool, the pool drawn and the drawn match.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lottery calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Winning odds are 1 to=(number of balls in the pool, balls to be drawn) ÷ ((balls to be drawn, number of matches) × (pool drawn, drawn match))
Winning odds are 1 to=pool drawn × (number of balls in the pool, balls to be drawn) ÷ (drawn match 1 × (balls to be drawn, number of matches) × (pool drawn, drawn match 1))
Number of matches=number of matches − 1
Winning odds are 1 to=((balls in the bonus pool, balls to be drawn) × (number of balls in the pool, balls to be drawn) ÷ ((balls to be drawn, number of matches) × (balls to be drawn, matches with bonus pool) × (bonus pool drawn, bonus match) × (pool drawn, drawn match)))
Number of balls in the pool=balls to be drawn + pool drawn
Drawn match 1=balls to be drawn − number of matches + 1

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lottery calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of matches, the matches with bonus pool and the pool drawn — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lottery calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of matches, the matches with bonus pool, the pool drawn and the drawn match, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Bonus match = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lottery calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
